passage: I'm Vinita, and I sit two rows behind Darshan in Class 6. He and Kunal have been best friends since Class 1. Then a new boy joined in July, and Kunal started sharing his tiffin with him. Darshan stopped eating his own lunch. Yesterday, when Kunal laughed at the new boy's joke, Darshan got up and left the bench. Today he told Kunal, loudly, that the new boy "copies everything." I can't know what he feels inside, but he keeps watching the two of them.

qa.q: When did the new boy join?
qa.a: In July.

qa.q: What might Darshan be feeling when he watches Kunal and the new boy?
qa.a: He seems jealous and afraid of losing his best friend to the newcomer.

qa.q: What would you advise Darshan to try instead of calling the new boy a copier?
qa.a: Tell Kunal honestly that he misses him, and try including the new boy rather than pushing him away.

qa.q: How might Kunal see Darshan's behaviour?
qa.a: Kunal may feel confused and hurt that his best friend is acting cold for no clear reason.

grounding: Shows a child fearing that a new classmate will take his best friend's place, seen by a classmate.

passage: The first week after her baby brother Thomas came home, Anjali, ten, watched relatives crowd round his cot. Nobody asked about her science prize. She slammed her door. The next Sunday, when Amma asked her to hold Thomas for a photo, she said, "Why? Everyone only cares about him." Two weeks later Amma sat with her alone and asked about the prize. Anjali talked for twenty minutes. That evening she held Thomas while Amma cooked, and he grabbed her finger.

qa.q: What prize had Anjali won?
qa.a: Her science prize.

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling when she said "Everyone only cares about him"?
qa.a: She felt jealous and hurt, afraid her baby brother had taken all the attention.

qa.q: What did Amma do that helped, and why?
qa.a: She made time for Anjali alone and asked about the prize, so Anjali felt she still mattered.

qa.q: What is it like for Amma to hear Anjali's words?
qa.a: It is probably painful and worrying, which pushes her to give Anjali time alone.

grounding: Shows a child's jealousy when a new baby takes family attention, easing when her mother makes time for her.

passage: "You think you're the only one who's felt this? When I, your Harish Dadu, was nine, my best friend was Sumit. We walked to school together every day. Then a boy from Bombay came, with a shiny compass box and stories about the sea. Sumit started walking with him. I was so afraid of losing Sumit that I told the teacher the new boy had broken my ruler. He hadn't. The teacher found out. That evening Sumit came to my house and said, 'You could have just walked with both of us.' So the next day, I did."

qa.q: What did the boy from Bombay have?
qa.a: A shiny compass box and stories about the sea.

qa.q: What was young Harish feeling when he lied to the teacher?
qa.a: He was jealous and afraid of losing Sumit to the new boy.

qa.q: What turning point in the story fixed things?
qa.a: Sumit coming to Harish's house and suggesting they all walk together.

qa.q: How might Sumit have felt when Harish lied about the new boy?
qa.a: Probably disappointed and a bit angry, but he still wanted to keep his old friend.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how as a child his fear of losing a friend to a newcomer led to a lie, and how the friend repaired things.

passage: "Listen, Arohi. When I, your Vaibhav Mama, was ten, a boy in my class got a red bicycle with gears. Gears! I had my father's old black one that squeaked. Every day I watched him ride past, and I wanted that bicycle more than anything. I even stopped saying hello to him. One day his chain came off near our house. I knew how to fix chains, from fixing mine every week. I helped him. He said, 'You're lucky you know how.' I'd never thought of myself as lucky before."

qa.q: What did the boy's bicycle have?
qa.a: Gears.

qa.q: How did young Vaibhav feel watching the red bicycle go past?
qa.a: He felt envious, wanting that bicycle more than anything.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed how Vaibhav saw things?
qa.a: When he fixed the boy's chain and heard he was lucky to have that skill.

qa.q: How might the boy with the red bicycle have seen Vaibhav?
qa.a: As someone skilled and helpful, maybe even someone to admire, not envy.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling a childhood envy of a classmate's bicycle and a moment that changed it.

passage: The football trials were on Saturday, and Siddharth, eleven, had only his old canvas shoes with a split toe. His family was saving for his sister's school fees, so new boots weren't possible. At practice, Thomas turned up in bright boots with studs, and everyone crowded round. Siddharth stared at them all through the warm-up and missed an easy pass. At home that night he stitched the split with his mother's thread and scrubbed the shoes white. "Skill, not boots," he muttered, though he didn't fully believe it.

qa.q: What did Siddharth use to stitch the split?
qa.a: His mother's thread.

qa.q: Why did Siddharth stare at Thomas's boots during warm-up?
qa.a: He felt envious, wishing he had boots like that and the attention they brought.

qa.q: What would you advise Siddharth before the trials?
qa.a: Focus on his passing and practice rather than the boots, and remember the coach watches how he plays.

qa.q: How might Thomas see his new boots?
qa.a: He may just be excited about them and not notice how they make Siddharth feel.

grounding: Shows a child envying a teammate's new boots when his own family cannot afford them.

passage: At the school annual day rehearsal, Yamini sang the solo, and everyone went quiet. Jyoti, twelve, sat in the chorus, mouthing the words. She'd always wanted a voice like that, and friends who crowded round her afterwards. On the bus home she told her mother, "Yamini has everything." That night she recorded herself singing in the bathroom and hated it. The next day she went to Yamini and said, "How do you breathe so long?" Yamini laughed. "I practise every morning. Want to come?"

qa.q: Where did Jyoti record herself singing?
qa.a: In the bathroom.

qa.q: What does Jyoti saying "Yamini has everything" suggest?
qa.a: She felt envious of Yamini's voice and popularity, and felt small next to her.

qa.q: Which choice by Jyoti helped, and why?
qa.a: Asking Yamini how she breathes, because it turned envy into learning.

qa.q: How might Yamini feel when Jyoti asks for her tips?
qa.a: Pleased and flattered, and happy to share her practice.

grounding: Shows a child envying a peer's talent and standing, then asking her for help.

passage: I'm Nilesh, Raghav's older brother. Raghav, eleven, has been trying to get into the colony football team for a year. Last week the captain finally said, "You're in." Raghav came home glowing. He wore the blue jersey to dinner and then to bed. Now he talks about "we" all the time: "We won," "We practise at six." He used to be quiet at family gatherings, but yesterday he told everyone about the match. I don't know exactly what it means to him, but he walks differently now.

qa.q: What colour is the team jersey?
qa.a: Blue.

qa.q: What does Raghav wearing the jersey to bed suggest?
qa.a: He feels proud and secure, deeply happy to belong to the team at last.

qa.q: How could Raghav's family support his new sense of belonging?
qa.a: Show interest in his matches and cheer for the team, while keeping home a place he's valued too.

qa.q: How does Nilesh see the change in Raghav?
qa.a: He notices Raghav is more confident and talkative, though he can only guess what it means inside.

grounding: Shows a child's joy and security at being accepted into a team, seen by an older brother.

passage: First week at the new school: Asif, ten, ate lunch alone under the stairs. Second week: Joseph, a boy from his class, asked, "You play carrom?" Asif joined their lunch group. He mostly listened. Fourth week: someone mentioned "the jalebi incident", and everyone looked at Asif and laughed, because it had been his joke. Asif laughed so hard his eyes watered. That night he told his mother, "I have a group now." He slept better than he had in months.

qa.q: What did Joseph ask Asif?
qa.a: "You play carrom?"

qa.q: How did Asif feel when everyone laughed at his old joke?
qa.a: He felt accepted and deeply happy, because the group now shared jokes that included him.

qa.q: What helped Asif move from eating alone to belonging?
qa.a: Joseph's simple invitation and Asif staying, listening and joining in over weeks.

qa.q: What might Joseph feel seeing Asif laugh with the group?
qa.a: Pleased and warm, glad that his invitation worked out.

grounding: Shows a child moving from loneliness to secure belonging in a peer group over a month.

passage: "Beta, I was eleven when we moved to the town, and no one talked to me. Then I saw girls playing kabaddi behind the school. Their captain was Rukmini, tall, with a loud laugh. I stood at the edge for three days. On the fourth, she shouted, 'Hey, new girl! We need one more!' I ran in, fell in the dust, and they all laughed, but not at me. After the game, Rukmini put her arm around my shoulders. That night I, your Farida Nani, cried from happiness. I still remember the smell of that dust."

qa.q: How many days did young Farida stand at the edge?
qa.a: Three days.

qa.q: Why did young Farida cry that night?
qa.a: She felt so happy and relieved to finally be accepted by the girls.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed things for Farida?
qa.a: Rukmini calling her in to play on the fourth day.

qa.q: How might Rukmini have seen the new girl at the edge?
qa.a: She probably noticed her waiting and wanted to include her, maybe remembering being new herself.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how as a child she found deep security in being accepted by a kabaddi team.

passage: Monday: Disha, ten, saw Afreen's notebook, neat handwriting, every sum ticked. She hid her own messy book under the desk. Wednesday: when the teacher read out marks, Afreen got nineteen out of twenty. Disha got twelve. She told her mother, "I'm the dumbest in class." Saturday: she asked Afreen how she wrote so neatly. "I copy it again at home," Afreen said. "My first try is messy too." Disha stared, then laughed a little. That night she rewrote one page slowly.

qa.q: What mark did Afreen get?
qa.a: Nineteen out of twenty.

qa.q: What does Disha saying "I'm the dumbest in class" suggest?
qa.a: She felt inferior and ashamed when she compared herself with Afreen.

qa.q: What small step helped Disha?
qa.a: Asking Afreen directly, and learning that the neat work came from effort, not magic.

qa.q: How might Afreen feel when Disha asks her?
qa.a: Maybe surprised that anyone envies her and glad to share her secret.

grounding: Shows a child feeling inferior when comparing herself with a classmate, then learning the gap came from effort.

passage: "Payal, you think you're not good enough? At twelve, I, your Ankita Masi, felt the same. My cousin Meena was top of her class, sang at every wedding, and everyone asked her to dance. At family dinners, I sat in the corner, feeling like nothing. One Diwali, Meena's grandmother fell ill, and I was the one who knew her medicines, because I always helped at home. Meena said, 'I could never remember all that.' I realised she wasn't better than me, just different. I still don't sing, though."

qa.q: What was Meena good at?
qa.a: She was top of her class, sang at every wedding, and everyone asked her to dance.

qa.q: How did young Ankita feel at family dinners?
qa.a: She felt inadequate and invisible, sitting in the corner comparing herself with Meena.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed Ankita's view?
qa.a: When she knew the grandmother's medicines and Meena admitted she couldn't do that.

qa.q: How might Meena have seen Ankita that Diwali?
qa.a: With new respect, seeing a skill in her she didn't have herself.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling feeling inferior to a cousin as a child and a moment that changed the comparison.

passage: The swimming gala was loud, crowded and running late. Abhinav, eleven, stood in lane four, shivering. On either side were boys who trained every morning. The whistle went. By the second length he could see their feet far ahead. He finished last. In the stands, parents cheered for others. He sat with a towel over his head. His friend Gurleen found him. "You beat your own time," she said, showing him her notebook. "By three seconds." He didn't look up. "Still last." But he took the notebook.

qa.q: Which lane did Abhinav swim in?
qa.a: Lane four.

qa.q: Why did Abhinav sit with a towel over his head?
qa.a: He felt inadequate and embarrassed after finishing last next to boys who trained more.

qa.q: What would you advise Abhinav after the gala?
qa.a: Compare himself with his own past times, like Gurleen did, and keep practising.

qa.q: What is it like for Gurleen to see Abhinav so low?
qa.a: She probably feels concerned and wants to show him his real progress.

grounding: Shows a child feeling inferior to faster peers after a race, with a friend pointing to his own improvement.

passage: "Saurabh, you're angry about the umpire? Let me tell you. When I, your Madhav Dadu, was ten, we played marbles every evening under the peepal tree. There was a boy who moved his marble closer when he thought no one saw. I saw. My face went hot, and I shouted, 'Cheat!' so loudly that the whole street stopped. He said I was lying. I didn't back down. I drew the line again in the dust and said, 'We start from here, properly.' The other boys agreed, and he played fair after that."

qa.q: Where did they play marbles?
qa.a: Under the peepal tree.

qa.q: What was young Madhav feeling when his face went hot?
qa.a: He was angry and indignant at seeing the boy cheat.

qa.q: What turning point in the story made the game fair again?
qa.a: Madhav redrawing the line and getting the others to agree to restart properly.

qa.q: How might the boy who cheated have felt when everyone agreed to restart?
qa.a: Probably embarrassed and exposed, which pushed him to play fair.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling his childhood anger at a peer's cheating and how he insisted on fairness.

passage: The inter-house race went on despite the rain. Naveen, eleven, was running second when he saw a boy ahead cut across the muddy corner behind the tree, where the teachers couldn't see. The boy finished first. Naveen crossed second, soaked and furious. "He cheated!" he told his friend Shankar, his fists clenched. "Everyone saw!" "The teacher didn't," Shankar said. Naveen marched to the PE teacher anyway, his voice shaking. "I'm not saying it for me. It's not fair to everyone else."

qa.q: Where did the boy cut across?
qa.a: The muddy corner behind the tree.

qa.q: Why were Naveen's fists clenched?
qa.a: He was furious and indignant that the boy had cheated and won.

qa.q: What could Naveen do to make his case clearly?
qa.a: Stay calm, describe exactly what he saw and ask the teacher to check with other runners.

qa.q: How might Shankar see Naveen's anger?
qa.a: He understands it, but worries it won't change anything since the teacher didn't see.

grounding: Shows a child's heated reaction to seeing a rival cheat in a race.

passage: At the society's Independence Day quiz, Sachin, twelve, noticed that the team from B-block kept looking at a man in the front row, who mouthed the answers. Sachin's ears went red. When B-block won, he stood up. "That's not fair! They were told the answers!" His sister Urmila tugged his sleeve. "Sit down, people are staring." "I don't care," he said. The organiser came over, listened, and agreed to hold a tie-break round with no one in the front row.

qa.q: What did the man in the front row do?
qa.a: He mouthed the answers.

qa.q: What made Sachin's ears go red?
qa.a: He felt angry and indignant about the cheating.

qa.q: What worked in Sachin's protest, and what could be better?
qa.a: Speaking up got a fair tie-break; he could have gone straight to the organiser rather than shouting.

qa.q: What is it like for Urmila when people stare?
qa.a: She probably feels embarrassed and anxious about the attention.

grounding: Shows a child's heated reaction to cheating at a community quiz.

passage: The hostel was cold that January, and Farhan, ten, had forgotten his sweater at home. He shivered through study hour. Tejas, from the next bed, said nothing but came back with his own spare sweater and put it on Farhan's desk. That evening Farhan also found Tejas had copied the maths notes he'd missed. Farhan held the sweater for a moment. "You didn't have to," he said. Tejas shrugged. "You'd do it." Farhan wrote him a note that night: "Thank you. I won't forget."

qa.q: What had Farhan forgotten at home?
qa.a: His sweater.

qa.q: What was Farhan feeling when he held the sweater for a moment?
qa.a: He felt grateful and touched that Tejas had noticed and helped without being asked.

qa.q: What could Farhan do to show his gratitude?
qa.a: Thank Tejas, as he did, and look for ways to help Tejas in return.

qa.q: How might Tejas feel reading Farhan's note?
qa.a: Warm and valued, glad his kindness mattered.

grounding: Shows a child recognising and thanking a hostel friend for deliberate kindness.

passage: I'm Irfan, Shreya's brother. Last week the school bus driver, Mahesh Uncle, waited five extra minutes when Shreya, who's nine, ran late because her shoe came off. The next day she made a thank-you card with a drawing of the bus and wrote, "Thank you for waiting for me." She gave it to him with a sweet. He smiled and put the card on his dashboard. I don't know exactly what she felt, but she talked about it all evening.

qa.q: How long did Mahesh Uncle wait?
qa.a: Five extra minutes.

qa.q: What might Shreya have been feeling when she made the card?
qa.a: She seemed grateful and warm, wanting to thank him for waiting on purpose.

qa.q: How could Shreya's parents encourage this habit?
qa.a: Notice and praise the card, and help her remember to thank people who help her.

qa.q: How does Irfan see Shreya's gratitude?
qa.a: He notices she talked about it all evening, which suggests it mattered to her.

grounding: Shows a child recognising a bus driver's deliberate kindness and thanking him, seen by her brother.

passage: September: Keerthana, from the next flat, started helping Jeevan, eleven, with fractions every Saturday. He came, but grumbled, checking the clock. October: he still sighed, but he started asking questions. November: the exam results came. Jeevan got his best maths mark ever. That evening he knocked on Keerthana's door with a box of barfi from his mother. "You gave up your Saturdays," he said, looking at his feet. "Thank you." Keerthana grinned. "You gave up yours too."

qa.q: When did Keerthana start helping Jeevan?
qa.a: In September.

qa.q: Why did Jeevan look at his feet when he thanked Keerthana?
qa.a: He felt grateful but a bit shy, maybe sheepish about grumbling before.

qa.q: What could Jeevan do to keep showing thanks?
qa.a: Keep working hard and maybe help another student, the way Keerthana helped him.

qa.q: How might Keerthana feel when Jeevan thanks her?
qa.a: Pleased and proud, seeing her Saturdays paid off.

grounding: Shows a child slowly recognising a neighbour's deliberate help and thanking her.

passage: At the school library, the rule was simple: one book at a time, and you queue. Deepak, eleven, was third in line when a Class 7 boy walked straight to the counter. Deepak stepped out. "There's a queue." The boy rolled his eyes. The librarian, Urmila Ma'am, looked up. "Deepak's right. Back of the line, please." The boy went. Deepak felt his chest swell. Later, he told his friends three times how he'd stood up for the rules.

qa.q: What was the rule at the library?
qa.a: One book at a time, and you queue.

qa.q: How did Deepak feel when Urmila Ma'am backed him?
qa.a: He felt proud and validated for upholding the rule everyone shared.

qa.q: What would you advise Deepak about telling the story three times?
qa.a: It's fine to feel proud, but he could stop there so he doesn't seem to be showing off.

qa.q: How might the Class 7 boy see Deepak?
qa.a: Probably as annoying or a goody-goody, at least at first.

grounding: Shows a child feeling validated by upholding a shared queue rule and being backed by an adult.

passage: I'm Trisha, and my brother Hemant, ten, became class monitor this term. At PE, the captains always picked their friends first. Hemant said, "Rule is: we count off, one-two, one-two." Some boys groaned, but the teacher agreed. The teams were even, and the match was close. Afterwards Hemant told us at dinner, "Everyone played properly for once." He was smiling all evening. I'm not sure if he was proud of the rule or of being monitor, but he seemed very sure he had done the right thing.

qa.q: How did Hemant say teams should be picked?
qa.a: By counting off, one-two, one-two.

qa.q: What might Hemant have felt at dinner?
qa.a: He seemed proud and satisfied that his fair rule worked.

qa.q: How could Hemant handle the boys who groaned?
qa.a: Explain that the rule gives everyone a fair chance, and keep applying it the same way for all.

qa.q: How does Trisha see Hemant's smile?
qa.a: Trisha wonders whether it is pride in the rule or in being monitor, but sees he feels sure he was right.

grounding: Shows a child feeling validated by enforcing a fair rule for his class, seen by his sister.

passage: Monday: in Class 7, Uma found a pencil box on the floor with money inside and handed it to the teacher, because that was the class rule. Everyone clapped. She felt warm all day. Thursday: in a game of kho-kho, Hrithik broke the rule by crossing early. Uma called it out loudly. He argued, but the group backed her. Next Monday: when a friend broke a small rule, Uma scolded her in front of everyone, and the friend cried. Uma felt the warm feeling turn uneasy.

qa.q: What did Uma find on the floor?
qa.a: A pencil box with money inside.

qa.q: Why did Uma's warm feeling turn uneasy on Monday?
qa.a: She began to feel guilty that her rule-keeping had hurt a friend, not just kept things fair.

qa.q: What would you advise Uma for next time?
qa.a: Point out small rule-breaking kindly and privately, so fairness doesn't turn into shaming.

qa.q: How might Hrithik see Uma after the kho-kho game?
qa.a: He may feel annoyed and see her as strict, even if the group agreed with her.

grounding: Shows a child feeling validated by upholding group rules over a week, then noticing its limits.

passage:
Badminton coach's note, Trisha, March
Gopika (11) lost the district final 21–8 on Saturday. She didn't cry on court, but she sat in the car park for a long time. On Monday she was the first to arrive at practice. She asked me to feed her smashes for half an hour, then worked on her footwork, which is what cost her the final. She's set herself a target: reach the next final in six months. I've made her a weekly plan and told her parents she's handling it well.

qa.q: What was the score in the district final?
What might Gopika have been feeling in the car park?
qa.a: Probably disappointed and hurt after the big loss, needing time to take it in.

qa.q: Why is Trisha's weekly plan a good support?
qa.a: It turns Gopika's determination into small, steady steps toward her long-term goal.

qa.q: How might Gopika's parents feel reading this note?
qa.a: Reassured and proud that she bounced back instead of giving up.

grounding: Shows a child bouncing back from a big loss and setting a long-term goal, noted by her coach.

passage:
Chetan's diary, Wednesday
Got my maths test back today: 9 out of 25. I wanted to disappear. I said nothing at dinner, and my sister Pallavi could tell. After dinner she sat with me and we went through every mistake. Most were the same one: I forget to carry numbers. So I made a plan. Ten sums every night, only carrying, until the next test. Pallavi says she'll check them. I'm still embarrassed, but I don't want to be the 9-out-of-25 boy. Day 1: done. 8 out of 10.

qa.q: What mark did Chetan get on the test?
qa.a: 9 out of 25.

qa.q: How was Chetan feeling after getting the test back?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and down, wanting to disappear.

qa.q: What made Chetan's plan a good one?
qa.a: It targets his main mistake with small daily practice he can keep up.

qa.q: How might Pallavi see Chetan's effort?
qa.a: She probably feels proud and wants to support him, which is why she offers to check his sums.

grounding: Shows a child recovering from a poor test score with a steady practice plan and his sister's help.

passage: In the hill town, the cycle race was down the steep road to the market. Tenzin, ten, crashed on the last bend and came fifth, with a scraped knee. His friend Omkar helped him push the cycle home. "Next year," Tenzin said, wincing. For three months he practised on that bend every evening, slowing, leaning, and trying again. He fell twice more. Omkar timed him with his father's watch. The next year he took the bend clean and finished second.

qa.q: Where did Tenzin crash?
qa.a: On the last bend.

qa.q: What does Tenzin saying "Next year" through his wince suggest?
qa.a: He felt hurt and disappointed, but also determined not to give up.

qa.q: What helped Tenzin improve?
qa.a: Practising the exact bend where he fell, steadily for months, with Omkar timing him.

qa.q: How might Omkar feel when Tenzin finishes second?
qa.a: Proud and happy, since he was part of the practice.

grounding: Shows a child bouncing back from a crash and working steadily for a year toward his goal.

passage: I'm Gargi, Pranav's sister. At dinner our uncle said, "Why did the tomato blush? It saw the salad dressing!" Last year Pranav, who's nine, would have asked what was funny. This time he burst out laughing, then said, "Mama, that joke is so old it's a fossil." Everyone laughed. When Uncle pretended to be hurt, Pranav said, "Just kidding," and gave him a high five. I can't be sure what he understands, but he seems to get the jokes now, and to know teasing from meanness.

qa.q: Why did the tomato blush in the joke?
qa.a: It saw the salad dressing.

qa.q: What might Pranav have felt when the family laughed at his fossil comment?
qa.a: He probably felt proud and pleased that his teasing joke landed.

qa.q: How could the family keep building Pranav's humour?
qa.a: Keep sharing puns and riddles and let him try making his own.

qa.q: How does Gargi see Pranav's change?
qa.a: She notices he gets jokes now and knows light teasing from meanness, though she can't be sure.

grounding: Shows a child understanding a pun and using light teasing without malice, seen by his sister.

passage: Monday: Siddharth told his sister Swati, eight, "Nice haircut, did you do it with a spoon?" Swati burst into tears and ran to Amma. Siddharth said, "I was joking!" Thursday: he asked her a riddle: "What has hands but can't clap?" She thought hard, then shouted, "A clock!" and grinned. The next Monday: he said, "Oh great, more homework, my favourite." Swati rolled her eyes. "You're being sarcastic." Then she added, "Nice hair, did you do it with a fork?" He laughed.

qa.q: What was the answer to Siddharth's riddle?
qa.a: A clock.

qa.q: How did Swati feel when she first heard the haircut joke?
qa.a: She felt hurt and upset, taking it as mean.

qa.q: What helped Swati understand the teasing?
qa.a: Playing riddles and hearing sarcasm in low-stakes moments helped her see the playful tone.

qa.q: How might Siddharth feel when Swati teases him back?
qa.a: Amused and relieved that she can now join in the joke.

grounding: Shows a child learning over a week to understand riddles, sarcasm and teasing without seeing malice.

passage: "Disha, I'll tell you about my maths teacher. When I, your Naveen Chacha, was ten, Rao Sir asked the class, 'Why was the six afraid of seven?' Nobody knew. He said, 'Because seven eight nine!' I didn't get it. The boys laughed, and I thought they were laughing at me. I sulked all day. The next morning Rao Sir wrote it on the board: seven ate nine. I suddenly saw it and laughed so loudly the class turned. Rao Sir winked at me. After that, I asked him for a new riddle every week."

qa.q: Why was the six afraid of seven, according to the riddle?
qa.a: Because seven eight nine.

qa.q: What was young Naveen feeling when the boys laughed?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and hurt, thinking they were laughing at him.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped Naveen get the joke?
qa.a: Rao Sir writing "seven ate nine" on the board the next day.

qa.q: How might Rao Sir have seen Naveen's sulking?
qa.a: He probably noticed Naveen had missed the joke and wanted to help him in on it.

passage: Week one: Bidisha and Parul, both ten, agreed to share Bidisha's cycle: half an hour each, turn by turn. Bidisha always brought it back on time. Week two: Parul kept it for an hour and said, "You didn't need it." Bidisha felt cheated but still returned it on time the next day. "If I break the rule, it stops working," she told her mother. Week three: Parul apologised. "You kept your side, so I'll keep mine." They wrote the rule on a card and stuck it on the cycle.

qa.q: How long was each turn with the cycle?
qa.a: Half an hour each.

qa.q: How did Bidisha feel when Parul kept the cycle for an hour?
qa.a: She felt cheated and hurt, but still wanted to keep her side of the deal.

qa.q: Which choice kept the deal alive, and why?
qa.a: Bidisha still returning on time, because it built trust and made Parul want to be fair too.

qa.q: How might Parul see the deal after week two?
qa.a: She realises Bidisha trusted her and feels she should keep her side.

grounding: Shows a child keeping a fair rule based on trust and reciprocity, even when her friend breaks it.

passage: "Hrithik, you asked why I always pay exactly. When I, your Farida Dadi, was eleven, the mango seller in our village left his basket and a tin by the road while he worked in the field. We children could take one mango and drop a coin in. One day my friend took two and paid for one. I said, 'If we cheat, he'll stop trusting us, and then no one gets mangoes.' She laughed at me, but she put the second coin in. That old man trusted us for years."

qa.q: Where did the mango seller leave his basket and tin?
qa.a: By the road.

qa.q: What might young Farida have felt when her friend took two mangoes?
qa.a: She felt uneasy and upset, worried that the cheating would break the seller's trust.

qa.q: What turning point in the story kept the system working?
qa.a: Farida speaking up and her friend paying the second coin.

qa.q: How might the mango seller have felt about the village children?
qa.a: He probably felt trusting and grateful, since they kept the honesty system for years.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling a childhood rule based on mutual trust and why keeping it mattered.

passage: On a hot afternoon the class teacher was called away, and the substitute didn't come. Class 7 was alone for forty minutes. There was one water cooler and thirty thirsty children. Arohi, twelve, stood near it. "One glass each, then back of the line," she said. Kavitha frowned. "Who made you boss?" "Nobody. It's just fair. We all need water." A few boys pushed, but most joined the line. When the teacher came back, the class was noisy but calm, and everyone had had water.

qa.q: How long was the class alone?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: What might Arohi have felt when Kavitha asked "Who made you boss?"
qa.a: She may have felt a little stung but stayed calm, sure that fairness mattered more.

qa.q: What made Arohi's rule work?
qa.a: It was simple, fair to everyone, and most children trusted it would give them a turn.

qa.q: How might Kavitha see Arohi's rule once she has had her water?
qa.a: She might accept it as fair, even if she didn't like being told at first.

grounding: Shows a child upholding a fair rule based on trust when no adult is present.
